note: Twelve school-level functional groups. Example molecules and reaction balances are checked by assets/scripts/validate-organic.cjs.

groups.name: Alcohol
groups.naming: Name the longest chain that includes the carbon bonded to OH, then end with -ol. Number the chain so the OH gets the lowest number (ethanol, propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol).
groups.explain: An alcohol has a hydroxyl group (–OH) bonded to a saturated carbon. The oxygen makes alcohols more polar than hydrocarbons of similar size.
properties: Lower alcohols are liquids and mix with water.
Burn in air to give carbon dioxide and water.
Alcohols other than methanol can be dehydrated to alkenes. Methanol has no neighbouring carbon from which to form a C=C bond.

reaction.title: Dehydration of ethanol
reaction.note: Water is removed and a C=C bond forms.

groups.advanced: Primary alcohols have the –OH on a carbon that is bonded to one other carbon (or to hydrogen in methanol). Secondary alcohols have the –OH on a carbon bonded to two carbons.

groups.name: Aldehyde
groups.naming: Name the chain including the carbonyl carbon and end with -al (methanal, ethanal, propanal). The carbonyl carbon is always carbon 1.
groups.explain: An aldehyde has a carbonyl group (C=O) with at least one hydrogen on that carbon, written –CHO.
properties: Small aldehydes are gases or volatile liquids.
The carbonyl group makes them reactive.
They burn in air.

reaction.title: Combustion of methanal
reaction.note: Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water.

groups.advanced: Aldehydes can be oxidised to carboxylic acids. That oxidation is often used as a classroom test.

groups.name: Ketone
groups.naming: Name the chain that includes the carbonyl carbon and end with -one. Number so the carbonyl gets the lowest number (propanone, butanone).
groups.explain: A ketone has a carbonyl group (C=O) bonded to two carbon atoms. There is no hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon.
properties: Propanone (acetone) is a common solvent.
Ketones are less easily oxidised than aldehydes under school conditions.
They burn in air.

reaction.title: Combustion of propanone
reaction.note: Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water.

groups.advanced: Because both sides of the carbonyl are carbon chains, ketones do not give the same simple oxidation tests as aldehydes.

groups.name: Carboxylic acid
groups.naming: Name the chain including the carboxyl carbon and end with -oic acid (methanoic acid, ethanoic acid).
groups.explain: A carboxylic acid has a carboxyl group (–COOH): a carbonyl and a hydroxyl on the same carbon.
properties: Weak acids: they turn blue litmus red.
Lower members are soluble in water.
React with alcohols to form esters.

reaction.title: Esterification
reaction.note: Ethanoic acid and methanol form methyl ethanoate and water.

groups.advanced: The carboxyl hydrogen is acidic because the anion left behind is stabilised by the neighbouring carbonyl group.

groups.name: Ester
groups.naming: Name the alkyl group from the alcohol first, then the acid part ending in -oate (methyl ethanoate, ethyl ethanoate).
groups.explain: An ester is formed from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. Many esters have fruity smells.
properties: Often pleasant-smelling liquids.
Do not turn litmus red (they are not acids).
Can be hydrolysed back to acid and alcohol.

reaction.title: Acid hydrolysis of methyl ethanoate
reaction.note: Acid hydrolysis gives ethanoic acid and methanol. Alkaline hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt, not the free acid, unless the mixture is acidified afterwards.

groups.advanced: In naming, the alcohol provides the alkyl prefix and the acid provides the -oate stem.

groups.name: Ether
groups.naming: Name the shorter alkoxy group, then the longer alkane (methoxymethane, methoxyethane, ethoxyethane).
groups.explain: An ether has an oxygen atom linking two carbon groups. There is no –OH hydrogen on that oxygen.
properties: Less polar than alcohols of similar size.
Ethoxyethane was once a common anaesthetic.
Burn in air.

reaction.title: Combustion of methoxymethane
reaction.note: Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water.

groups.advanced: Ethers are isomers of alcohols with the same molecular formula, but they lack the hydrogen-bonding –OH group.

groups.name: Amine
groups.naming: Name the chain and end with -amine, or use the alkanamine form (methanamine, ethanamine).
groups.explain: A primary amine has an –NH2 group bonded to a carbon. Amines are related to ammonia.
properties: Often have a fishy smell.
Act as weak bases.
Lower members are gases or volatile liquids.

reaction.title: Reaction of methanamine with hydrogen chloride
reaction.note: The amine accepts a proton and forms methanaminium chloride, CH3NH3Cl.

groups.advanced: Primary, secondary and tertiary amines differ by how many carbon groups are attached to nitrogen. This Lab shows primary amines only.

groups.name: Amide
groups.naming: Name the chain including the carbonyl carbon and end with -amide (methanamide, ethanamide).
groups.explain: An amide has a carbonyl group bonded to a nitrogen. Primary amides end in –CONH2.
properties: Many are solids at room temperature.
The –CONH2 group can hydrogen-bond.
Acid hydrolysis gives a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt.

reaction.title: Acid hydrolysis of ethanamide
reaction.note: The amide bond breaks to give ethanoic acid and ammonia (as an ammonium salt in acid). Alkaline hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt and ammonia.

groups.advanced: The amide link is the same kind of bond that joins amino acids in proteins.

groups.name: Haloalkane
groups.naming: Name the halogen as a prefix (chloro-, bromo-) on the alkane name (chloromethane, chloroethane, bromoethane).
groups.explain: A haloalkane (alkyl halide) has a halogen atom bonded to a saturated carbon. X stands for F, Cl, Br or I.
properties: Often denser than water.
Do not mix well with water.
Can take part in substitution reactions.

reaction.title: Substitution of chloromethane
reaction.conditions: Warm water (school overview of the organic change)
reaction.note: Chlorine is replaced by OH and hydrogen chloride forms. In the laboratory the usual reagent is warm aqueous alkali, which gives a chloride salt instead of HCl.

groups.advanced: In many school courses the reagent is written as aqueous sodium hydroxide; the organic change is still replacement of X by OH.

groups.name: Nitrile
groups.naming: Count the carbon of the –CN group in the chain and end with -nitrile (ethanenitrile, propanenitrile).
groups.explain: A nitrile has a carbon–nitrogen triple bond. The carbon of –CN is part of the parent chain for naming.
properties: Contain a polar C≡N bond.
Can be reduced to amines.
Useful building blocks in organic synthesis.

reaction.title: Reduction of ethanenitrile
reaction.note: The triple bond is reduced and ethanamine forms.

groups.advanced: Older names such as acetonitrile are still common in laboratories for ethanenitrile.

groups.name: Alkene
groups.naming: Name the chain that includes the double bond and end with -ene. Number so the double bond gets the lowest number (ethene, propene, but-1-ene).
groups.explain: An alkene is an unsaturated hydrocarbon with a carbon–carbon double bond. The double bond is the functional group.
properties: More reactive than alkanes.
Decolourise bromine water.
Take part in addition reactions.

reaction.title: Addition of bromine
reaction.note: Bromine adds across the double bond and the orange colour fades.

groups.advanced: Displayed formulas in this Lab are flat and do not show cis/trans isomers.

groups.name: Alkyne
groups.naming: Name the chain that includes the triple bond and end with -yne. Number so the triple bond gets the lowest number (ethyne, propyne, but-1-yne).
groups.explain: An alkyne is an unsaturated hydrocarbon with a carbon–carbon triple bond.
properties: Unsaturated and reactive at the triple bond.
Decolourise bromine water.
Can be hydrogenated to alkenes and then alkanes.

reaction.title: Hydrogenation of ethyne
reaction.note: Enough hydrogen converts ethyne all the way to ethane.

groups.advanced: Partial hydrogenation can stop at the alkene if the conditions are controlled.
